sysd-msg-143.title: Loose coupling: changing one part without breaking the rest
sysd-msg-143.text:
A change in one component should disturb the others as little as possible. That is the promise of loose coupling. A loosely coupled system is one whose components make little or no use of knowledge of the definitions of other components. A loosely coupled component can be replaced by another implementation of the same service.

In code, a class that depends only on an interface can be served by any implementing class. A new class replaces the old without changing the dependent one. In distributed systems, loose coupling comes from transactions, queues in message-oriented middleware and interoperability standards. Publish–subscribe gives the highest level of decoupling. Synchronous patterns such as RPC, a call that runs a function on another machine, create tightly coupled components. Services stay loosely coupled when they pass only key data. A letter-sending service takes a customer identifier and looks up the address itself.

Loose coupling has a price. Decoupling in time makes transactional integrity hard and needs extra coordination protocols. Replication creates consistency issues. An asynchronous caller can overload the recipient until it fails.

sysd-msg-091.title: Monolithic application: one unit that does everything
sysd-msg-091.text:
A monolith is built as a single unit and handles every step needed to satisfy a business need, not one particular task. For a small team with little complexity, it is still a good choice. It is relatively simple and low cost. Development and debugging are simple, communication is fast and reliable, testing is easy, and ACID transactions are supported.

The trouble grows with the codebase. Maintenance gets harder, the application is tightly coupled and hard to extend, and it commits the team to a particular technology stack. The whole application is redeployed on each update, and a single bug can bring down the entire system. Monoliths lack elasticity, scalability and the ability to survive faults. Once one becomes too complex, it can be refactored into {{ref:sysd-msg-083}} or a distributed application.

Even on a single machine, a monolith may be performant enough for the current workload. Yet it is less available, durable, changeable and scalable than a well-designed distributed system. Common architectural patterns for monoliths, each with trade-offs, are layered architecture, the {{ref:sysd-msg-077}} and microkernel architecture.

sysd-msg-083.title: Microservices: small services that scale on their own
sysd-msg-083.text:
A monolith that supports three functions must be scaled in its entirety, even if only one function is under strain. Microservices avoid that. The architecture organizes an application into a collection of small, loosely coupled services that communicate through lightweight protocols. Teams can develop, deploy and scale each service independently, so only the strained function's service is scaled out.

There is no universally agreed definition. Each service is generally designed around one business capability, inside the boundary of one domain model (see {{ref:sysd-msg-085}}), with its own codebase managed by a small team. Small is a matter of responsibility, not size. Each service also persists its own data, a database per service, unlike the traditional model where a separate data layer handles persistence.

The benefits follow from independence. Services deploy independently, give multiple teams agility, improve tolerance of faults and data isolation, and remove any long-term commitment to a particular technology stack. The costs are just as real. They are the complexity of a distributed system, harder testing, expensive maintenance, challenging communication between services, problems keeping data correct and consistent, and network latency and congestion.

The complexity of a monolith does not disappear when it is split into services. Some of it becomes operational complexity, so teams need decentralized delivery (see {{ref:sysd-reliab-143}}) and DevOps, with holistic watching of every service.

sysd-msg-094.title: Service-oriented architecture: building from services that already exist
sysd-msg-094.text:
The aim is to build applications purely from existing services. Service-oriented architecture, or SOA, focuses on discrete services instead of a monolithic design (see {{ref:sysd-msg-091}}). It is intended to be independent of vendors, products and technologies, and is a good choice for system integration. One definition gives a service four properties. It represents a repeatable business activity with a specified outcome, is self-contained, is a black box to its consumers, and may be composed of other services.

SOA promotes reuse at the macro, service level rather than the class level. A service treated as a project separate from its consumers can be delivered quickly and independently. That also encourages good design, because the service is designed without knowing who its consumers are.

SOA can be implemented with web services or microservices. It has costs. Without compact, binary ways of calling a service remotely, applications could run more slowly and need more processing power. Stateful services reduce the provider's scalability if it must keep each consumer's context, and they increase coupling. Testing is hard, because there is no uniform testing framework.

sysd-msg-092.title: Service discovery: finding services that keep moving
sysd-msg-092.text:
In a monolith, parts call each other with ordinary method or procedure calls. Microservices have no such luxury. They run in virtualized or containerized environments. There the number and location of service instances change dynamically, so clients need a way to reach a changing set of ephemeral instances.

Service discovery is the answer. It automatically detects devices and services on a network, which reduces the manual configuration effort required from users and administrators. A service discovery protocol is a network protocol that helps accomplish it. It needs a common language, so software agents can use one another's services without continuous user intervention. Many protocols exist, including DNS Service Discovery and Simple Service Discovery Protocol. Another example is {{ref:sysd-reliab-050}}, which provides two modes of service discovery, using environment variables or its own DNS.

sysd-msg-093.title: Service mesh: a proxy beside every service
sysd-msg-093.text:
As the number of services grows, routing the calls between them becomes increasingly complex. A service mesh makes it managed, observable and secure. It is a dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication, and it gives visibility into communications, secure connections, and automated retries and backoff for failed requests.

It has two parts. Network proxies paired with each service form the data plane, and a set of management processes forms the control plane. The data plane intercepts and processes calls between services. The control plane coordinates the proxies and provides APIs to manipulate and observe the whole network.

Each service instance is paired with a {{ref:sysd-blocks-137}} called a sidecar, which shares its container and is managed by an orchestration tool such as {{ref:sysd-reliab-050}}. The sidecars can support service discovery, load balancing and secure communications, including checks on who a caller is and what it may do. Istio, Cilium, Linkerd and {{ref:sysd-msg-144}} implement the architecture, and many meshes use the Envoy proxy on the data plane.

sysd-msg-145.title: Distributed tracing: following one request through many services
sysd-msg-145.text:
When one user request passes through many services, finding the slow or failing one is hard. A distributed trace helps. It is an interrelated series of discrete events, called spans, that track the progression of a single request through the services that fulfil it. A trace shows the causal and temporal relationships between the services.

Spans carry unique identifiers that let a tracing backend build parent-child relationships between them, and span information is typically passed in the HTTP headers of outbound requests. Instrumenting an application means sending span information to the backend, which correlates the spans into traces. The main way to view a trace is a swimlane view, as in Jaeger.

Tracing is mainly used for anomaly detection, fault analysis, debugging and diagnosis. It has overhead, so in production there is a trade-off between how fine-grained the tracing is and its cost. It can also generate a large volume of messages, so it must often be possible to switch it off, at compile time or at run time. OpenTelemetry is a CNCF open source project that supports it.

sysd-msg-080.title: N-tier architecture: layers in the code, tiers on the machines
sysd-msg-080.text:
Layers and tiers sound alike, but one is a design and the other is a place. Layers divide an application logically, each with a specific responsibility. They manage dependencies: a higher layer can use services in a lower layer but not the other way around. Tiers are physically separated and run on separate machines. A tier can call another directly or use asynchronous messaging, and several layers may share one tier. Separating tiers physically improves scalability and resiliency but adds latency from the extra network communication.

Layers can be closed or open. In a closed layer architecture a layer can call only the next layer down, which limits dependencies but may create unnecessary network traffic. In an open one it can call any layer below.

The widely used 3-tier design has three layers. A presentation layer handles user interactions, a business logic layer validates data, and a data access layer operates on the database. In 2-tier, the presentation layer runs on the client and talks to a data store, with no business logic layer. In single-tier, everything runs on one application or server.

The advantages are improved availability, firewall-like layers for security, independent scaling of tiers and easier maintenance by different people. The disadvantages are added complexity, network latency that grows with the number of tiers, a hardware cost per tier, and harder network security.

sysd-msg-078.title: Orchestration versus choreography: who decides the order
sysd-msg-078.text:
Two services must cooperate on one job. Who decides the order? In choreography, nobody does. Service choreography describes the exchange of messages and the rules by which the microservices interact, with point-to-point communication between them. In orchestration, a central orchestrator acts as the center of authority. It is responsible for invoking and combining the services, and it describes the interactions between all participating services. The orchestration pattern also includes transaction management among different services.

Each style wins somewhere. Orchestration is more reliable because it has built-in transaction management and error handling, while choreography's point-to-point communication makes scenarios where services fail much more complicated. Orchestration also scales more easily in one respect. Adding a service means only the orchestrator changes its interaction rules, whereas in choreography all the interacting services must change.

Orchestration pays for this. It adds latency, because all services talk through the central orchestrator, and throughput is bound to the orchestrator's capacity. The orchestrator is also a single point of failure: if it goes down, no services can talk to each other, so it must be highly available. Netflix Conductor is a real-world microservice orchestrator.

sysd-msg-097.title: Microservices versus SOA: a question of scope
sysd-msg-097.text: Microservices and SOA are sometimes used interchangeably, but they differ, and the main distinction comes down to scope. SOA defines how to make software components reusable through service interfaces and common communication standards. Microservices are many smallest independent service units, aimed at team autonomy and decoupling. Another view calls microservices a modern interpretation of SOA, a new implementation approach popular since 2014 that stresses continuous deployment and agile practices. Among their characteristics the literature lists fine-grained interfaces, business-driven development and lightweight container deployment.

sysd-msg-096.title: Service provider, broker and consumer
sysd-msg-096.text: Each SOA building block can play any of three roles: service provider, service broker or service requester, which is the consumer. The broker is also called a registry or repository. The provider creates a web service and gives its information to the service registry. The broker makes information about the service available to any potential requester. Public brokers are available everywhere, while private brokers reach a limited public. A consumer locates entries in the broker's registry with find operations. It then binds to the provider to invoke its web services, under a standardized service contract with business, functional and technical parts.

sysd-msg-095.title: Service-oriented design principles
sysd-msg-095.text: No industry standard fixes the exact composition of a service-oriented architecture, but many sources have published their own principles. Services adhere to a standardized service contract. They stay loosely coupled through reference autonomy, where services only know of each other's existence. They also use location transparency, where a service can be called from anywhere in the network. Services act as black boxes that hide their inner logic. They are autonomous over the functionality they encapsulate, and stateless, returning a value or an exception to minimize resource use. They should be long lived, composable into other services, discoverable through communicative metadata, and divided to promote reuse of code.

sysd-msg-082.title: Service registry and registration: the address book of instances
sysd-msg-082.text: If service instances come and go, someone must keep the address book. That is the service registry: a database containing the network locations of service instances that clients can reach. It must be highly available (see {{ref:sysd-scale-068}}) and up to date. Instances get into it in one of two ways. With self-registration, an instance registers and de-registers itself, and may send heartbeat requests to keep its registration alive. With third-party registration, the registry tracks running instances by repeatedly checking the deployment environment or subscribing to events. It records newly available instances and de-registers terminated ones.

sysd-msg-079.title: Components of a microservice architecture
sysd-msg-079.text:
A set of microservices usually sits among a handful of supporting components. A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend services. A CDN, a group of geographically distributed servers holding static content, is checked first by clients before they reach the backend.

The API gateway handles incoming requests and routes them to the relevant services. It talks to service discovery and to a component that confirms who users are and what they may do (see {{ref:sysd-reliab-026}}). Services register themselves in the service registry and discovery component, which the gateway searches to find the services it needs to talk to. A management component monitors the services. Microservices are designed and deployed in different domains, and each domain has its own database.

sysd-msg-081.title: Client-side and server-side discovery
sysd-msg-081.text: Once instances have registered their locations, a client has two ways to find one. In client-side discovery, the client obtains a service's location by querying a service registry that manages and stores the network locations of all services. In server-side discovery, the client sends its request to an intermediate component, such as a load balancer, which forwards it to an available service instance. The difference is who does the lookup: the client, or something in between. Tools used to implement service discovery include Eureka, Apache ZooKeeper, {{ref:sysd-msg-144}} and {{ref:sysd-reliab-058}}.

sysd-msg-074.title: Microservices best practices
sysd-msg-074.text:
Most rules for good microservices come down to one: keep them independent. Model services around the business domain (see {{ref:sysd-msg-127}}), with loose coupling and high functional cohesion, and make each do one thing well. Each service owns and manages its own data, kept private to it, so coupling falls and services can evolve independently. Shared database schemas are a cause of coupling. Services should communicate only through well-designed APIs, avoid leaking implementation details and keep API changes backward compatible. Services should talk over lightweight protocols, and the options include {{ref:sysd-msg-002}}, {{ref:sysd-msg-005}} or message brokers.

Design for failure at infrastructure, database and service levels, with bulkheads, {{ref:sysd-reliab-067}} or {{ref:sysd-reliab-084}}, and fail fast so failures do not cascade. Retry policies and caching improve availability. A large attack surface calls for security at every level of the communication path, and with many services centralized logging becomes critical for finding issues. Containerization deploys microservices in isolation and simplifies their scaling and deployment.

sysd-msg-073.title: Monolith versus microservices: start simple, or split early?
sysd-msg-073.text:
Should a new system begin as a monolith or as microservices? Plainly, it depends on team size, business maturity and latency needs. Singh's guide advises starting with a monolith when building a new system, while accepting that each approach has its own advantages and disadvantages.

Microservices are not a silver bullet. They solve an organizational problem, and adopting them is about organizational priorities and team structure as much as technology. Questions to ask before moving include whether the team is too large for a shared codebase and whether teams are blocked on other teams. Others are whether microservices bring clear business value, whether the business is mature enough, and whether the current architecture limits the team through communication overhead. Not every application must be broken up. Microservices are solutions to complex concerns, and a business without such concerns does not need them.

Latency can settle the matter outright. Latency-sensitive applications such as real-time gaming, at millisecond latency, and low-latency trading, at microsecond latency, avoid microservices because network latency between separate processes is unbearable. Microservices are usually stateless, with state kept in a database, but gaming and trading keep state in memory for quick updates. These applications also talk to the server at high frequency and must reach the same running instance, so they need web socket connections and sticky routing.

sysd-msg-085.title: Bounded context: where one model holds
sysd-msg-085.text: Inside a bounded context, one domain model is consistent and valid. It is a core idea of domain-driven design, and it defines an area that ensures clarity and separation of concerns. A bounded context often maps to a microservice, and a one-to-one mapping is typically ideal, because it keeps clear boundaries, reduces coupling and enables independent deployment and scaling. One context may be split into several microservices for varying scalability needs, or several contexts consolidated into one microservice for simplicity or lower operational overhead. The choice should balance domain-driven design principles with business goals, technical constraints and operational requirements.

sysd-msg-086.title: Cell-based architecture: limiting the blast radius
sysd-msg-086.text: Cell-based architecture organizes computational resources into self-contained cells. Each cell operates independently on a subset of requests, while the design keeps scalability, fault isolation and availability. A cell typically holds multiple microservices and acts as an autonomous unit. Entire sets of microservices may be replicated across cells, so requests can be rerouted to another working cell on failure, which limits the impact of localized failures. The pattern in {{ref:sysd-reliab-067}} works at two levels here. Inside a cell it stops failures spreading among microservices, and between cells it isolates a failing cell and redirects traffic to the remaining ones.
